Almost everything most people know about John and Priscilla comes from a poem.
In Longfellow’s The Courtship of Miles Standish, the widowed Captain Standish, braver in battle than in courtship,
sends his young friend John Alden to ask for Priscilla’s hand on his behalf.
Alden loves her himself, and delivers the message anyway.
She hears out his long praise of the captain and answers with the most famous line in the poem.
It was a bestseller at once, and for a century American schoolchildren learned it by heart.
No record from Plymouth tells the story.
It first reached print in 1814, when the Reverend Timothy Alden set it down as an “anecdote,
which has been carefully handed down by tradition” in the family, and added that “the captain never forgave him to
the day of his death”. That part at least is doubtful: Standish and Alden settled side by side at Duxbury,
and Standish’s son Alexander married the Aldens’ daughter Sarah.
Longfellow was writing about his own people.
His mother, Zilpah Wadsworth, descended from John and Priscilla through their daughter Elizabeth Pabodie,
the same daughter this family comes from, which makes the poet a distant cousin.
